draft.title: Using quotations as evidence
card: A quotation is the exact words from a text, placed inside quotation marks. Use it as evidence to back up your claim.
Keep it short. Pick only the few words that prove your point, rather than a whole sentence or passage.
Weave the quotation into your own sentence so that it reads smoothly, for example: The poet calls the sea "a hungry beast", which suggests danger.
Always explain what the quotation shows. Name a word or technique in it and say what it makes the reader think or feel.
draft.remember: Keep the quotation short, fit it into your sentence, then explain what it shows.

a.q: Which sentence uses a quotation in the best way?
opts: The storm is "a roaring giant", which makes it seem powerful
The storm is shown. "A roaring giant." That is the quotation
The poem has a storm in it and it is "a roaring giant"
"The storm was a roaring giant over the town all night"
a.why: The first sentence weaves a short quotation into the sentence and explains what it shows. The third fits the words in but never says what they show. The others drop the words in on their own or copy a long line with no explanation.
a.clue: Look for a short quotation that is fitted into the sentence and explained.

b.q: Sam writes: Mr Hale is unkind because he "never smiled at anyone". What should Sam add to finish the evidence?
opts: An explanation of what the words show about Mr Hale
A longer quotation copied from the next paragraph
A second quotation with no comment on either one
A summary of the whole book from start to end
b.why: Sam has woven in a short quotation, but has not said what it shows. A sentence explaining that never smiled suggests coldness would complete it. Adding more quotations without comment repeats the same gap.
b.clue: The quotation is in. What does it prove?
